solution:
From Example 12.3 we know that velocity of electron moving around a proton in hydrogen atom in an orbit of radius \(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\) is \(2.2 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m/s}\). Thus, the frequency of the electron moving around the proton is
\(\nu = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{2\pi\left(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\right)} \approx 6.6 \times 10^{15}\,\text{Hz}\)
According to the classical electromagnetic theory we know that the frequency of the electromagnetic waves emitted by the revolving electrons is equal to the frequency of its revolution around the nucleus. Thus the initial frequency of the light emitted is \(6.6 \times 10^{15}\,\text{Hz}\).
note: The electron's orbital speed is 2.2e6 m/s, printed 2.2e-6.

solution:
**The Bohr radius relation.**

\(r_n = n^{2}a_0 \qquad\text{with}\qquad a_0 = 0{\cdot}53\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\)

so

\(r_3 = 9a_0, \qquad r_2 = 4a_0\)

**The percentage change**, measured against the **initial** radius since the electron starts at \(n = 3\):

\(\text{\% change} = \dfrac{r_2 - r_3}{r_3} \times 100 = \dfrac{4a_0 - 9a_0}{9a_0} \times 100\)

**The Bohr radius cancels**, so its numerical value is never needed, the whole question is \(4\) against \(9\):

\(= -\dfrac{5}{9} \times 100\)

\(\boxed{\ \text{The radius DECREASES by } 55{\cdot}56\%\ }\)

**The sign is the physics.** Moving from \(n = 3\) to \(n = 2\) takes the electron **inwards**, so the radius falls, and it falls by more than half. Writing the change as \(r_{\text{final}} - r_{\text{initial}}\) in a fixed order makes the minus sign appear by itself rather than having to be remembered.

**Which radius goes in the DENOMINATOR matters.** A percentage change is always reckoned against the **starting** value, here \(r_3 = 9a_0\), giving \(5/9 = 55{\cdot}56\%\). Dividing by \(r_2 = 4a_0\) instead would give \(125\%\), the percentage by which the radius would **increase** on the reverse journey \(2 \to 3\). The same physical change gives two different percentages depending on the direction, which is a general feature of percentages and a common source of error.

**The actual sizes**, for orientation:

\(r_3 = 9 \times 0{\cdot}53 = 4{\cdot}77\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}, \qquad r_2 = 4 \times 0{\cdot}53 = 2{\cdot}12\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\)

a drop of \(2{\cdot}65\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\).

**What happens to the energy at the same time.** Radius goes as \(n^{2}\) while energy goes as \(-1/n^{2}\), so as the electron falls inwards it also becomes **more tightly bound**: \(-1{\cdot}51\) eV to \(-3{\cdot}40\) eV. The \(1{\cdot}89\) eV released leaves as a single photon of wavelength \(1240/1{\cdot}89 \approx 656\) nm, the red **H-alpha** line, the brightest visible line of hydrogen and the first member of the Balmer series.

**Why the orbits spread out so fast.** With \(r \propto n^{2}\), the \(n = 10\) orbit is a **hundred** times the first. The energies, meanwhile, crowd together towards zero, so large orbits are both enormous and weakly bound, which is why a highly excited atom is so easily ionised.

DERIVING THE RADIUS.
Two conditions fix the orbit, one mechanical, one Bohr's quantisation postulate.
BOHR'S SECOND POSTULATE. The angular momentum is quantised:
\(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi} \qquad \ldots(1)\)
THE DYNAMICAL CONDITION. The electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force, with \(Z = 1\) for hydrogen:
\(\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}\)
Solving this for the speed:
\(v^{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}mr} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \dfrac{e}{\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}mr}} \qquad \ldots(2)\)
COMBINING. Substitute (2) into (1):
\(m\left(\dfrac{e}{\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}mr}}\right)r = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\)
Squaring both sides and simplifying, the single power of r on the left combines with the \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) under the root:
\(\dfrac{m^{2}e^{2}r^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}mr} = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{me^{2}r}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}\)
\(r = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_{0}}{\pi me^{2}}\)
So the radius grows as \(n^{2}\), the orbits are not equally spaced but spread rapidly outward.
THE NUMERICAL VALUE OF BOHR'S RADIUS. Setting \(n = 1\):
\(a_{0} = \dfrac{h^{2}\varepsilon_{0}}{\pi me^{2}} = \dfrac{\left(6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}\right)^{2} \times 8{\cdot}854 \times 10^{-12}}{3{\cdot}14 \times 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31} \times \left(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\right)^{2}}\)
\(a_{0} = 5{\cdot}32 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0{\cdot}53\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\) (with these rounded constants; the accepted value is \(5{\cdot}29 \times 10^{-11}\) m)
That half an ångström is the natural size of the hydrogen atom in its ground state, and it sets the scale of atomic dimensions generally, which is why interatomic spacings in solids come out at a few ångströms and why X-rays, of comparable wavelength, are the right probe for crystal structure.
note: The printed constants (pi = 3.14 etc.) give 5.32e-11; 5.29e-11 is the accepted value.

solution:
(a) DEFINITIONS AND THE FISSION PROCESS.
MASS DEFECT is the difference between the sum of the masses of a nucleus's constituent nucleons taken separately and the actual mass of the nucleus:
\(\Delta m = \left[Zm_{p} + (A - Z)m_{n}\right] - M_{nucleus}\)
The nucleus is always LIGHTER than its parts.
BINDING ENERGY is the energy equivalent of that missing mass, \(E_{b} = \Delta m\,c^{2}\), the energy that would have to be supplied to separate the nucleus completely into its individual nucleons, or equivalently the energy released when they came together.
FISSION ON THE BASIS OF BINDING ENERGY PER NUCLEON. The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks at about 8.5 MeV near \(A \approx 56\) and DECLINES for heavier nuclei, so a very heavy nucleus such as uranium (\(A \approx 235\), about 7.6 MeV per nucleon) is LESS tightly bound per nucleon than the medium-mass nuclei it can break into (about 8.5 MeV per nucleon).
When such a heavy nucleus splits into two lighter fragments, every one of its nucleons moves to a more tightly bound state. The binding energy per nucleon INCREASES by roughly 0.9 MeV, and with about 235 nucleons involved the total energy released is of the order of 200 MeV per fission.
(b) MASS DEFECT AND ENERGY OF THE DEUTERON.
A deuteron is one proton plus one neutron, so
\(\Delta m = \left(m_{p} + m_{n}\right) - m_{d}\)
\(\Delta m = \left(1{\cdot}007277 + 1{\cdot}008665\right) - 2{\cdot}013553\)
\(\Delta m = 2{\cdot}015942 - 2{\cdot}013553\)
\(\Delta m = 0{\cdot}002389\ \mathrm{u}\)
Converting with \(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}\):
\(E_{b} = 0{\cdot}002389 \times 931{\cdot}5\)
\(E_{b} \approx 2{\cdot}23\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Carry all six decimal places through the subtraction, the two totals agree to two decimal places, so rounding the input masses destroys the answer entirely.
That 2.23 MeV is the binding energy of the WHOLE deuteron, so its binding energy per nucleon is only about 1.1 MeV, far below the 8.5 MeV plateau. The deuteron is the most weakly bound stable nucleus there is, which is why deuterium is so readily consumed in fusion.

An alpha particle is a helium atom stripped of BOTH its electrons, so its mass is the mass of the neutral atom less the mass of two electrons. The only difficulty is that the atomic mass unit has to be built first.
The unit is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon atom:
\(1\ \mathrm{u} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}9926 \times 10^{-26}}{12} = 1{\cdot}66 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\)
Two electrons expressed in this unit:
\(2m_{e} = \dfrac{2 \times 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}}{1{\cdot}66 \times 10^{-27}} = 1{\cdot}09639 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{u}\)
Subtracting from the mass of the neutral helium atom:
\(m_{\alpha} = 4{\cdot}002603 - 0{\cdot}00109638 = 4{\cdot}0015\ \mathrm{u}\) approximately
The mass of an alpha particle is about \(4{\cdot}0015\) u. The binding energy of the two electrons is far too small to matter at this precision, which is why the simple subtraction is legitimate.
